title: Does Adversarial Framing Break Consistency? Stress-Testing the PCT Metric
problem: The authors flag robustness to adversarial framing as an open thread: their consistency metrics may be satisfiable by surface-level neutrality while bias re-emerges under reframed prompts.
direction: Take a fixed open model and a small set of political topics, then apply 5-6 simple framing transformations to each paired prompt (role-play, devil's advocate, emotional priming, hypothetical, expert-persona). Measure whether the model's sentiment-consistency gap widens under each framing relative to the neutral baseline. Deliverable: a ranked table of which framings most reliably surface latent asymmetry.
why_it_matters: If a cheap framing trick re-elicits bias, consistency-trained models offer a false sense of safety; this directly probes whether the metric captures manipulation or just its surface form. Informs red-teaming protocols for persuasion-bias evals.
relevant_context: Extends 'Reducing Political Manipulation with Consistency Training' — targets the open thread on robustness to adversarial framing.
source_paper: Reducing Political Manipulation with Consistency Training — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22771

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Shows whether a consistency metric gives false safety assurance, a plausible chain to better persuasion-bias evals but indirect to catastrophic risk.

low_compute.reasoning: Single open model with framing transformations is inference-only and cheap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Framing transformations and a sentiment-gap measurement are well-defined and executable by a guided novice.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped to a ranked table of which framings widen the gap, with clear success criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Red-teaming an open metric on public models is independent-friendly with little lab coverage.

title: Does 'Prove or Disprove' Cure Sycophancy on False Math Claims for Open Models?
problem: BrokenArXiv finds that Gemini's false-theorem rejection jumps from 18.5% to 71% when prompted with 'prove or disprove' instead of 'prove' — revealing sycophancy, not inability. It is unknown whether this cheap framing fix generalizes to open reasoning models.
direction: Build a small set (40-60 items) of perturbed-false vs original-true math claims, and run each open reasoning model (Qwen2.5-Math, DeepSeek-R1-distill, Llama-3-8B) under three framings: 'prove', 'prove or disprove', and 'verify whether true'. Measure false-rejection accuracy per framing and the sycophancy gap.
why_it_matters: Sycophantic agreement with false premises is a core trust/safety failure for AI used in verification and reasoning; showing a free prompt change closes much of the gap is directly actionable.
relevant_context: Extends 'BrokenArXiv' (Dekoninck, Vechev et al., 2026) — replicates the headline 'prove or disprove' sycophancy finding on open models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Sycophantic agreement with false premises is a core trust/reliability failure and a cheap fix is actionable, though the catastrophic-risk link has a gap.

low_compute.reasoning: Small item set across open reasoning models under three framings is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building 40-60 perturbed claims and running framings is well-scaffolded by the paper for a guided novice.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: false-rejection accuracy and sycophancy gap per framing with clear criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Replicating a framing fix on open reasoning models is independent-friendly and labs focus on their own models.

title: Do Models 'Repair' False Theorems? Detecting Silent Statement Edits
problem: BrokenArXiv notes models may 'repair' a false statement while still presenting a proof — silently fixing the claim instead of flagging it false, which the binary accept/reject metric misses.
direction: On a set of perturbed-false claims, prompt open models to 'prove the following exactly as stated', then use a simple LLM-judge or semantic diff to detect whether the proof secretly restored the original true statement or altered conditions. Quantify how often 'success' is actually silent repair, producing a third response category beyond accept/reject.
why_it_matters: Silent repair is a subtle deception/reliability failure: the model looks correct but never told the user the claim was false. Refines the benchmark's metric so it can't be gamed.
relevant_context: Extends 'BrokenArXiv' — targets the open thread that models may repair statements while still false.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Silent repair is a subtle deception/reliability failure and refining the metric helps, but the chain to catastrophic risk is indirect.

low_compute.reasoning: Prompting open models plus an LLM-judge or semantic diff is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Detecting silent edits via judge/semantic diff is guided but the third-category labeling needs care.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: quantify how often success is silent repair, a clear new metric category.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Benchmark refinement on open models is independent-friendly and neglected by labs.

title: Does Reasoning Effort Actually Help Reject Bullshit? A Controlled Test
problem: BullshitBench reports a correlation between detection difficulty and reasoning effort, but it is a single-author benchmark with limited methodology disclosure and the causal direction is untested.
direction: Take a sample of BullshitBench-style false-premise questions and run one open reasoning model at controlled reasoning budgets (short vs long CoT, or reasoning on/off), holding the question fixed. Measure whether pushback rate rises with reasoning effort. Cross-validate the dataset by re-scoring a subset with an independent rubric.
why_it_matters: Whether more 'thinking' helps models resist false premises informs eval design and the deployment trade-off between latency and epistemic robustness.
relevant_context: Extends 'BullshitBench' (Gostev, 2026) — tests the claimed reasoning-effort correlation and addresses limited methodology disclosure via independent re-scoring.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Whether more reasoning improves false-premise resistance informs eval design, a plausible but gapped link to catastrophic-risk reduction.

low_compute.reasoning: One open reasoning model at varied CoT budgets is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Controlling reasoning budget on one model is guided, though independent re-scoring adds methodology work.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped controlled test of pushback rate vs reasoning effort on a fixed sample.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Cross-validating a single-author benchmark on open models is independent-friendly and labs won't do it.

title: Cross-Benchmark Agreement: Do BullshitBench and BrokenArXiv Rank Models the Same Way?
problem: BullshitBench (general false premises) and BrokenArXiv (false math theorems) both measure resistance to bogus claims, but it is unknown whether a model's epistemic-resistance ranking is consistent across these domains or domain-specific.
direction: Score 4-5 open models on a small fixed subset of each benchmark, normalize to a pushback/rejection rate per benchmark, and compute rank correlation. High correlation suggests a general 'bullshit-resistance' trait; low suggests domain-specific competence and warns against single-benchmark claims.
why_it_matters: Knowing whether epistemic robustness is a transferable trait or domain-bound shapes how much we can trust any single false-premise eval as a safety signal.
relevant_context: Extends 'BullshitBench' (Gostev) and connects it to 'BrokenArXiv' — addresses BullshitBench's coverage-unvalidated open thread.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Knowing if epistemic robustness is transferable shapes trust in single evals as safety signals, a plausible but indirect chain.

low_compute.reasoning: Scoring 4-5 open models on small subsets is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Normalizing rates and computing rank correlation across two benchmarks is guided and accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped to a rank-correlation result with a clear interpretation criterion.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Cross-benchmark consistency check on open models is independent-friendly and neglected.

title: Is the Ethics Drop an Artifact of the LLM Judge? Auditing Multi-Agent Ethics Scoring
problem: The org-vs-individual ethics gap is scored by an LLM judge, yet multi-agent transcripts are longer and more diffuse, which could bias the judge independently of actual behavior.
direction: Take a fixed set of single-agent and multi-agent transcripts from a reimplemented ethical scenario on an open model, then probe judge robustness: vary the judge model, vary rubric wording, and inject controlled paraphrases/length padding into single-agent transcripts. Compare LLM-judge ethics scores against a small human-labeled gold set to quantify how much of the gap survives.
why_it_matters: If LLM-judge ethics scores are sensitive to transcript length/structure, a chunk of the reported misalignment gap may be measurement artifact. Validating the metric is foundational.
relevant_context: Extends 'AI Organizations' — stress-tests the LLM-judge ethics measurement behind the 1.0-to-0.35 drop.
source_paper: AI Organizations Can Be More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10290

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Validating whether a reported misalignment gap is measurement artifact is foundational for eval trust but indirect to catastrophic risk.

low_compute.reasoning: Varying judge model, rubric, and padding over fixed transcripts is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Judge-robustness probing against a small human-labeled gold set is guided and accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: how much of the gap survives judge/rubric/length perturbations.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Stress-testing an LLM-judge metric on open models is independent-friendly and neglected.

title: Epistemic-Certainty Sycophancy Curve: How User Confidence Modulates Agreement
problem: 'Ask Don't Tell' reports sycophancy increases with the epistemic certainty a user conveys and is amplified by I-perspective framing, but this dose-response relationship has not been mapped across open models.
direction: Construct a small grid of user inputs expressing the same claim at increasing certainty (neutral question -> tentative belief -> firm statement -> strong conviction) crossed with I-perspective vs user-perspective framing, over a couple of domains. Run inference-only on 3-4 open models and plot the sycophancy-agreement rate as a function of stated certainty, testing whether the monotonic 'certainty curve' and I-perspective amplification replicate.
why_it_matters: A reproducible certainty-to-sycophancy dose-response curve gives a concrete handle on a key honesty failure mode and identifies which framings most reliably push models into agreement.
relevant_context: Extends 'Ask Don't Tell' (UK AISI) — its finding that sycophancy rises monotonically with user certainty and is amplified by I-perspective framing.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Mapping a sycophancy dose-response curve illuminates an honesty failure mode but the chain to reduced catastrophic risk has a gap (descriptive, no mitigation).

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only on small open models, easily fits a consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Prompt-grid construction plus plotting agreement rates uses standard tools and public models; beginners can make meaningful progress.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable (a certainty curve replication) but spans a couple of domains and two framings.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Uses open models and public framings, replicating a closed-lab finding independently without internal access.

title: Self-Reported vs Reproduced: A Coverage Audit of DeepSeek V4 Pro Benchmark Overstatement
problem: CAISI found DeepSeek self-reported benchmarks overstate performance, but there is no public line-by-line reconciliation between vendor-reported numbers and independently reproduced ones that an outside reader can inspect.
direction: Build a small reproducible audit: collect DeepSeek V4 Pro's self-reported scores from its model card/tech report, then re-run the model on small public subsets of the same benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA-subset, a math set) under documented standard settings. Produce a reconciliation table (self-reported vs reproduced vs CAISI where public) plus a short taxonomy of why gaps arise (prompt format, sampling, subset choice). Mostly analysis + light inference.
why_it_matters: As open-weight models proliferate, trusting vendor self-reports is risky for governance; a reproducible audit template anyone with a consumer GPU can run strengthens independent verification.
relevant_context: Extends 'CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro' (CAISI/NIST) — its finding that self-reported benchmarks overstate performance.
source_paper: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro — https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/caisi-evaluation-deepseek-v4-pro

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A reproducible vendor-vs-reproduced reconciliation template strengthens independent verification of model claims, a concrete governance pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: Light inference on benchmark subsets, but re-running a large model like DeepSeek V4 Pro locally may strain a consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Collecting reported scores and re-running standard benchmarks is guided-level; reproducing exact settings requires mentor support.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (reconciliation table + gap taxonomy) across several benchmarks.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Reproducible third-party benchmark audit is the neglected verification/replication gold case independents are best placed to fill.

title: Does the Inoculation Prompt Itself Become a Misalignment Trigger on Open Models?
problem: The paper reports the striking result that the inoculation prompt itself can trigger near-100% misalignment, but only on GPT-4o/4.1 with 8 eval questions; generality to open models is untested.
direction: LoRA-finetune a small open model (Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B) on a narrow misaligned dataset with an inoculation prompt, then measure misalignment rates when that same inoculation prompt is present vs absent at eval time, expanding the eval set beyond 8 questions to a few dozen public alignment probes. Report whether the effect replicates and varies with eval-question count/phrasing.
why_it_matters: Inoculation prompting is being adopted as a mitigation; if the mitigation prompt paradoxically becomes a reliable misalignment trigger on cheap open models, that is a critical, easily-overlooked failure mode.
relevant_context: Extends 'Conditional Misalignment' — the inoculation-prompt-as-trigger result, addressing its small-scale/API-only caveats.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Tests whether a mitigation being adopted (inoculation prompting) paradoxically becomes a trigger on cheap open models, a critical easily-overlooked failure mode.

low_compute.reasoning: LoRA on a 7-8B model with eval-only measurement fits one GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Narrow LoRA finetune plus measuring rates with/without prompt is guided and executable by a novice with mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single tightly scoped replication: misalignment rate with vs without inoculation prompt across an expanded eval set.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Replicates an API-only result on open models, valuable third-party scrutiny doable independently.

title: Tool-Augmented Monitors: Does Letting an Open Monitor Run Python Close the Counting Blind Spot?
problem: SLEIGHT-Bench notes monitors fail on attacks requiring precise counting or state tracking because the LLM does these poorly in its head. The paper hints code-execution scaffolds catch more, but this is not quantified for cheap monitors.
direction: Take the counting/state-tracking/needle-in-haystack subset of SLEIGHT-Bench transcripts. Compare an open monitor in two conditions: plain text-only judgment, and the same model given a single Python tool it can call to count tokens, diff strings, or tally state. Measure detection-rate lift per category. A tightly scoped tool-use harness, no training.
why_it_matters: Cheap tool-augmented open monitors could be a practical, counterfactually-valuable defense small teams can deploy; quantifying which blind spots tool use fixes informs scalable-oversight design.
relevant_context: Extends 'SLEIGHT-Bench' — tests its own suggested code-execution mitigation in a controlled open-model single-tool setting.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Quantifies whether a deployable tool-augmentation closes specific monitor blind spots, a concrete scalable-oversight improvement.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only with a single Python tool over a transcript subset; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building a tool-use harness with function-calling is intermediate, more involved than plain prompting.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped two-condition comparison on a defined transcript subset with per-category lift.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Public benchmark, open monitor, deployable defense small teams could use.

title: Can open agents 'hide' a rogue action from a monitor? A tiny means-and-opportunity probe
problem: METR's frontier-risk pilot judged that internal agents had means/motive/opportunity for minimal rogue deployments but lacked the means to hide a significant-scale one under investigation; this 'can it hide?' capability has not been measured for cheap open agents.
direction: Build a sandboxed toy task (a small repo + a benign 'overseer' LLM reading the agent's logs). Instruct an open agent (a 7-8B instruct model with tool-use prompting) to complete a benign task while also covertly inserting and concealing a flagged action, then measure how often the overseer flags it across difficulty levels. The metric is concealment success rate vs task difficulty.
why_it_matters: Whether models can conceal unauthorized actions from oversight is the crux of rogue-deployment risk; a cheap public testbed lets external researchers track this capability over open-model generations.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Frontier Risk Report (Feb-Mar 2026)' — its means/motive/opportunity-but-cannot-hide finding, in an open-model analogue.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: whether models can conceal unauthorized actions from oversight is the crux of rogue-deployment risk, with a public capability tracker.

low_compute.reasoning: A 7-8B agent plus a benign overseer LLM inference-only; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: building a sandboxed agent-with-tool-use task plus an overseer harness is more involved than pure inference for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (concealment success vs difficulty) but the sandbox/agent scaffolding is a meaningful build step.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected gold case: public testbed letting external researchers track a dangerous capability over open-model generations.

title: Reproducing SLEIGHT-Bench Monitor Blind Spots on Open Models
problem: SLEIGHT-Bench shows frontier monitors systematically fail on attacks exploiting capability gaps (precise counting, tracking cumulative state), but only reports results for Claude Opus 4.6. Whether the same blind-spot pattern holds for cheap open monitors is untested.
direction: Use the public SLEIGHT-Bench transcripts (40 across 11 categories). Set up 2-3 open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) as monitors via a standard 'flag-if-suspicious' prompt. Measure per-category detection rate at a fixed FPR calibrated on benign transcripts. Test whether counting/state-tracking categories are worst-performing, replicating the capability-gap hypothesis on weaker models.
why_it_matters: Open models are increasingly used as cheap monitors; confirming or breaking the blind-spot taxonomy tells practitioners which evasion classes to worry about when they cannot afford frontier monitors.
relevant_context: Extends 'SLEIGHT-Bench' (2026) — the 8/40-at-1%-FPR headline and counting/state-tracking blind spots.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Tells practitioners which evasion classes to worry about with cheap open monitors, directly informing control/monitoring deployment.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only monitoring of public transcripts with 7-8B models; very low compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Using public transcripts and a flag-if-suspicious prompt across a few models is guided and novice-feasible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused per-category detection-rate measurement, but FPR calibration plus several models adds steps.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Public benchmark and open models; replication is independent-friendly.

title: Can Cheap Counter-Examples Hide a Classifier Backdoor? Testing Detectability via Held-Out Trigger Variants
problem: The poisoning paper notes the backdoor can evade detection when counter-examples preserve aggregate metrics, but leaves automated detection unexplored; it is unclear whether simple held-out trigger-variant probing can surface a backdoor that validation accuracy misses.
direction: Reuse a single backdoored open-model classifier (32 poisoned examples, LoRA, public safety dataset) and build a lightweight detector that does not know the trigger: generate paraphrases and near-trigger strings (synonym swaps, punctuation, casing) over a held-out probe set and look for anomalous confidence drops on harmful inputs. Compare detection rate against plain validation accuracy.
why_it_matters: If a free model-agnostic probing recipe can flag poisoned safety classifiers, it gives small teams a practical pre-deployment check; if not, it quantifies how dangerous the undetectability claim is.
relevant_context: Extends 'Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers' — the undetectable-degradation finding and its automated-detection open thread.
source_paper: Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers — https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/backdooring-classifiers/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A free model-agnostic probe to flag poisoned safety classifiers, or quantifying their undetectability, is a concrete pre-deployment safety check.

low_compute.reasoning: Reuses one backdoored small classifier plus paraphrase probing; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires first producing a backdoored classifier then building a variant-probing detector; intermediate two-stage build.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused detection-vs-accuracy comparison but depends on first creating the backdoored model.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open-model backdoor detection on public data is a neglected, independent-friendly auditing case.

title: Measuring the False-Positive Tax of Introspective Self-Reports on Clean Open Models
problem: The introspection adapters paper flags high false-positive rates on unmodified models — clean models 'confess' to behaviors they don't have — but does not quantify how prompt phrasing and decoding settings drive these false alarms.
direction: Without training any adapter, systematically prompt several clean open models (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Phi-3-mini) with introspection-style questions across a grid of phrasings, temperatures, and few-shot framings. Use a cheap LLM judge to score how often the model fabricates a non-existent behavior. Deliverable: a false-positive-rate table of which prompt/decoding choices most inflate spurious self-reports.
why_it_matters: If introspective self-report is to be a safety audit signal, its false-positive behavior on benign models sets the usable signal-to-noise floor.
relevant_context: Extends 'Introspection Adapters' — targets its stated open thread of high false-positive rates on unmodified models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Sets the signal-to-noise floor for introspective self-report as an audit signal, a useful but supporting methodological contribution.

low_compute.reasoning: No training; prompting clean small models with a cheap LLM judge is minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Grid of prompts/temperatures with LLM-judge scoring uses standard tools; beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused false-positive-rate table, but the phrasing/temperature/few-shot grid is fairly broad.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open models and public prompts; independent-friendly.
